news.title: MI offer came out of the blue, says Uthappa
news.excerpt: New batting coach of the franchise says his endeavour will be to bring clarity among the star batters like Rohit, Suryakumar and Tilak
news.author: Vijay Tagore
body: For Robin Uthappa the Mumbai Indians job came out of the blue. Although he had been yearning for a role in the IPL, he was still taken by surprise.

“It came completely from left field. I didn't see it coming. The interest was there, though. I've been hoping that I would get a call at some point to work with a franchise because I felt I could add a lot of value,” the former India batter says.

Mumbai Indians recently announced Uthappa (41) as the batting coach in a setup headed by Kieron Pollard. “So, when the call came, the conversations happened. The interest was there from my side. I think there is a wealth of experience from playing in the IPL over so many years,” Uthappa, who featured in 46 ODIs and 13 T20Is, says reflecting on the job.

He was part of the MI team in the league's inaugural season. Ahead of the second season, he was traded to Royal Challengers Bengaluru in exchange for Zaheer Khan. Since then, he played for four more franchises – Kolkata Knight Riders, Rajasthan Royals, Chennai Super Kings and Pune Warriors. He won the IPL titles with KKR in 2012 and with CSK in 2021. In all he has played 205 IPL games.

Uthappa moved to Dubai three years ago and has since been undertaking individual coaching assignments rather than group sessions. Some of the cricketers he works with, he claims (without disclosing names), are current India internationals.

At MI, he will be working with established India stars and World Cup winners, like Rohit Sharma, Suryakumar Yadav and Tilak Varma, among others. The endeavour, he notes, will be to bring clarity to their thinking

“As established cricketers, having clarity is important. Nobody is bigger than Mother Cricket. I think everyone has been in the game long enough to know that nobody can beat Mother Cricket or supersede it. You can be as established as you want, but as athletes, you always want to have clarity before a tournament begin.

“There are a lot of things that established players require, and as coaches, we can serve them by making sure that we give them everything they need to feel ready to perform. They should feel happy and confident about where they are before a match begins. Sometimes, just being available is such a big blessing for established players. There are umpteen things you can do.”

He continues, “They don't think of themselves as World Cup champions or as captains who have won it five times. That kind of achievement adds a lot of value when you look at it from a team perspective. But you won't find individual cricketers thinking, 'I am a World Cup-winning captain. I don't need to hear anything.' Everyone is really humble.”

MI do not have explosive batters with strike rates of around 250, like Sunrisers Hyderabad and Rajasthan Royals do in Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Will they have to change their personnel? Uthappa believes that such qualities can be discovered in the existing players too.

“Honestly, I think the talent is already there in the existing side. There is enough and more talent to prove that these players are worth their weight in gold. They are capable of performing exceptionally well. I think it depends on the conversations you have with the existing players.

“(Besides) there is an auction coming up, so you have to see what possibilities there are, perhaps, to pick up one of them,” he remarks, stating something that was never heard of before about the five-time champions, “As Mumbai Indians, we feel like we are underdogs.”

news.title: MI Emirates avenge loss to Desert Vipers
news.excerpt: Kusal Perera hit 58 and put up a 94-run opening stand with Muhammad Waseem (41 off 30) to set up the massive win for the Kieron Pollard-led side
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: MI Emirates avenged their Season 4 final defeat against Desert Vipers with an emphatic 52-run victory in the opening match of ILT20 Season 5. At the Dubai International Stadium on Saturday, Kusal Perera hit 58 and put up a 94-run opening stand with Muhammad Waseem (41 off 30) to set up the massive win for the Kieron Pollard-led side.
Chris Jordan (4/19) and Zahoor Khan (3/13) bowled the Vipers out for 122 after MI Emirates batters, having been put into bat, posted 174 for eight.

Perera and Waseem gave MI Emirates a flying start, while the Vipers' chase never recovered from the loss of Fakhar Zaman early on. Joe Clarke's 35 off 28 balls, with five fours, was the Vipers' best effort, but they lost four wickets for 17 runs in a middle-overs collapse that decided the contest.

"I backed my strengths whenever the ball was in my area. I've been working on this for the last two to three years. The pressure is high in leagues, but we try to express ourselves, and the management encourages us to play that way," Player of the Match Kusal Perera, who smashed six fours and two sixes in his 40-ball 58, said.

Desert Vipers skipper Shadab Khan their bowling was not up to the mark initially. "We were too loose in the first 10 overs and gave away too many runs, but we recovered well as a group. Our bowling was better in the second half, and the pitch seemed to hold up a lot in the second innings. We all know how good Naseem Shah (2/24) is, and he has been showing that quality all year."

Brief Scores: MI Emirates 174/8 (Kusal Perera 58, Muhammad Waseem 41, Nicholas Pooran 32, Naseem Shah 2 for 24, Khuzaima Tanveer 2 for 40) beat Desert Vipers 122 in 19.1 overs (Joe Clarke 35, Shimron Hetmyer 21, Vriitya Aravind 21, Chris Jordan 4 for 19, Zahoor Khan 3 for 13) by 52 runs.

news.title: From learner to learning tree: KL Rahul's Test evolution
news.excerpt: With confidence in his game and clarity in his role, Rahul has become the steadying influence in a young Indian batting line-up
news.author: Bharat Sundaresan
body: On the day he scored his first Test hundred in New Zealand, KL Rahul was asked why he thought he’d been batting with an average nearly 10 runs higher than his Test average over the last two years.
“Because I’ve scored more runs, Sir,” Rahul said very matter-of-factly and with no fuss before elaborating a bit more, this time almost apologetically.

It was an innocuous answer to a rather innocuous question. But like everything else he mentioned during his rather insightful press conference; this too was a great reflection of Rahul’s presence frame of mind in Test cricket. His confidence, his self-assuredness and his clarity.

KL Rahul has found himself. Not just within himself but within this Test team. But most importantly also as a Test batter. He’s scored centuries before in much tougher conditions and against much more challenging bowling attacks.

But his maiden Test ton in his maiden Test innings on New Zealand shores, the 13th overall of his career, stamped him as being the big brother of this Indian Test batting line-up. One in which he is the only player in his 30s, and at 34 a senior figure too.

There have been so many different versions of Rahul the Test batter since he made his debut at the MCG in December 2014, the last one for MS Dhoni in the format for good measure, and only a year removed from the retirement of Sachin Tendulkar. The prodigiously talented right-hander with a familiar name who was set to take the world by storm in his early 20s, to his various iterations through various comebacks into the Test team. This current run though has not only been among his longest but also by far his most profitable. And even as opener, he's seen some major departures around him.

He's now the oldest member of a batting line-up that’s taking shape and coming into its own as he only seems to be flourishing in that role. It’s showing in the way he goes about his batting too. There’s the same lack of fuss around it as there is in the way he talks about it.

And he brings the same sense of self-assuredness to it too. He’s precise in the way he leaves the ball, and he did that excellently well against a largely disciplined New Zealand attack on a pitch which is designed for the bowlers to toil away. It’s one truism that has stood the test of time in Test cricket. The best openers often tend to be the best leavers of the cricket ball.

And Rahul’s attractive strokeplay in a wonderfully-crafted Test century was only as impressive as his ability to resist not getting greedy on a surface which was leaden with temptations, especially once the bowlers started to tire. His only real shot in anger came very late in the piece, a handful of deliveries before he got out, off a hapless Jacob Duffy who was given the thankless task of bowling halfway down the slow pitch.

It's quite telling that Rahul’s most prolific partnership in Test cricket so far has been with Yashasvi Jaiswal. The classic yin and yang where Rahul’s serenity at one end blends nicely with the mercurial nature of his younger partner. But in a way, it seems to have brought the best out of Rahul. It’s quite a feature of their stands in the middle where Rahul walks down to Jaiswal, every time the left-hander has had one of those moments where he’s let his natural aggression get the better of him. It’s never a stern word or even a piece of advice but more a reminder that he’s there to back him up. As if he’s saying, “you keep doing what you do, I’m here for you.”

It's also how he went about building a vital second-wicket partnership with Devdutt Padikkal playing only in his fifth Test. Especially when the tall and elegant No 3 was battling away at the start of his innings. Rahul ensured that he faced a lot of the deliveries off the likes of Matt Henry and Kyle Jamieson so that Padikkal could find some rhythm and flow. And it worked. With Shubman Gill, he’s happy to take the backseat and let his young captain dictate terms in setting the pace for the Test match.

What hasn’t changed is the overall class of Rahul with the bat. Whether it was the two shots through the off-side to kickstart proceedings on Day 3, one in front of square off the front foot followed by a late cut to the right of the backward point field, or a couple of late flourishes against Glenn Phillips on the back of some excellent use of his feet.

For years, Rahul had to exist in the shadows of some high-profile Test teammates, but now he is the learning tree that the others thrive on. And more so, it’s a position in the team that he seems to be thriving on as well. It’s allowing him to evolve and find himself while he helps those around him do the same in their own journeys of development.

news.title: England pick uncapped Ben McKinney for SA tour
news.excerpt: The young Durham opener was been picked after Jacob Bethell was ruled out of the tour
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: England have called up 22-year-old Durham opener Ben McKinney for their upcoming three-match Test series against South Africa. McKinney’s maiden international call-up comes after Jacob Bethell was ruled out of the tour due to a knee injury.

A left-handed batter, McKinney made his first-class debut for Durham in 2023, aged 18. He has since played 40 first-class matches, scoring 2389 runs at an average of 37.92. He was Durham's leading run-scorer and the third-highest overall in the previous County Championship Division Two season, finishing with 1044 runs from 14 matches at an average of 52.20.
Picked for the England Lions in 2024 with just three first class games under his belt, McKinney has been on England’s radar.
Additionally, the youngster also has experience playing on South African soil, having captained England Under 19 during the 2023-24 Under 19 World Cup in the country.
England will begin their tour with a three-day warm-up fixture against CSA XI in Durban before the first Test at The Wanderers in Johannesburg on December 17.

Updated England squad: Joe Root (c), Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Sonny Baker, Harry Brook, Sam Cook, Jordan Cox, Ben Duckett, Emilio Gay, Dan Lawrence, Liam Patterson-White, Ollie Robinson, Jamie Smith, Josh Tongue, Ben McKinney

news.title: SRH teammate says Cummins will turn up for IPL
news.excerpt: Additionally, Josh Hazlewood and Cameron Green are expected to be available for their respective franchises
news.author: Vijay Tagore
body: Pat Cummins, at the centre of the resurfaced Sandpapergate controversy, is expected to feature in IPL 2027. The Australia captain, who received a vote of confidence from Cricket Australia (CA) on Saturday, is believed to have confirmed his availability for the season, even as a couple of key Australian players have opted out, citing workload concerns. Josh Hazlewood, however, will turn up for Royal Challengers Bengaluru.

Cummins is the captain of Sunrisers Hyderabad (SRH), and the fact that the franchise has not released him is an indication of his availability. Now, a senior member of the side has also confirmed that he is expected to turn up. “I have spoken to Pat and he has said he will come for sure, if not for the whole season, at least for a part of it,” the member, who is currently part of the ILT20 in the UAE, told Cricbuzz.

It has also been the franchise's consistent position that the skipper would be available for the season, which was why he was not released. Cummins featured in only part of last season, joining the team in the second half after receiving a late go-ahead from CA. He played eight games, with Ishan Kishan leading the side in his absence.

Cummins' availability was in doubt because of Australia's packed international schedule on either side of the IPL. Australia are scheduled to play nine Tests before the IPL, including five against India between January and March, followed by a five-Test Ashes series against England immediately after the league, from June to August. However, those doubts over his participation have now been put to rest.

SRH, however, have had to release Head after the opener decided to focus on family and international commitments. Delhi Capitals are in a similar situation, having had to release Mitchell Starc after the pacer expressed his inability to take part in the season. The veteran quick wants to manage his workload.

However, Hazlewood is believed to have conveyed his availability to Royal Challengers Bengaluru, the two-time defending champions. Cameron Green, too, is expected to be available for the season, according to Kolkata Knight Riders, who retained him. “We have been told that he will come for the season,” a KKR official said, explaining the decision not to release the all-rounder, who was bought by the franchise for a whopping Rs 25.20 crore at the last auction.

news.title: Khaled backs Bangladesh to bounce back after Johannesburg defeat
news.excerpt: With Hasan Mahmud ruled out, Bangladesh are looking to regroup and address their bowling shortcomings ahead of the second Test
news.author: Atif Azam
body: Bangladesh pace bowler Khaled Ahmed said on Saturday (November 21) that they are looking to put behind their nine-wicket defeat at Johannesburg as they prepare to take on South Africa in the second Test, scheduled to be played in Centurion from November 23.

Bangladesh, who were humbled in the opening Test, are focusing on bouncing back in the second, and that too without in-form pace bowler Hasan Mahmud, who has been ruled out of the series after injuring his right elbow in the opening game.
“I think there is no point thinking about what has gone. Everyone is thinking about how we will go forward,” said Khaled at Centurion on Saturday.

“Everyone is trying to overcome it (the first Test defeat) and the practice is going well. Certainly it is a bad thing for us (missing Hasan) as he is an important bowler and now that he is not around certainly we will miss him,” he said.
Khaled added that the side is taking input from the local coaches in their dressing room to gain an understanding of what to expect in Centurion.

Bangladesh recently appointed assistant coach Malibongwe Maketa, while his compatriot, South African all-rounder Dale Benkenstein, joined the team as a batting specialist during their tour of South Africa.
“We have two South African coaches here, and we are discussing with them how to play in these conditions," he said.
Khaled said that sitting on the bench is always painful but added that he is always ready to seize his opportunity whenever it comes.

“I don't know (why I am not picked as it is the decision of the team management and the captain),” said Khaled. “Since I have played county, my rhythm is good and if I get the opportunity, I will try to do well.

“Sitting out is of course painful, but it is about the combination of the team and the decision of the team management. I am always ready to play and if my chance comes I will definitely give 100 percent and try to give my best,” he said.
Khaled added that maintaining a disciplined length was key for fast bowlers in South Africa.

The Bangladesh side was criticised for bowling too short in the Johannesburg defeat, with commentators, including former South African bowler Shaun Pollock, saying that Bangladesh had bowled too many back-of-a-length balls.

“The most important thing for pace bowlers to succeed is to maintain the length,” said Khaled, who was among Bangladesh's best bowlers on their previous tour. If we can hold the length for a long time without trying too many things, I think the chance of success is higher,” he said.

“The wicket here is a bit higher, so there was an adjustment issue. Maybe our bowlers were a little late to adjust, so a few short balls were bowled. But I think everyone will come back very well in this match,” he said, adding that the bounce in the wicket might have prompted the pacers to try too hard in the opening Test, forcing them to bowl too many no-balls.

“The wicket is a bit bouncy and the effort to hit hard grew too big, and we didn't adjust. Our bowlers don't bowl so many no-balls easily. Maybe it (no-balls) happened a bit more in this match," he said.

news.title: Lehmann denies knowledge of sandpaper plot
news.excerpt: The former Australia coach also spoke about the mental and emotional toll of the 2018 scandal
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Darren Lehmann, Australia's head coach at the time of the 'Sandpapergate' scandal, has once again denied any knowledge of the plot. Speaking on ABC's broadcast during the first T20I between Australia and England, Lehmann said his “version stays the same” and reiterated that he “didn't know” sandpaper would be used.
“The biggest thing with ball tampering is [that] it was just a bad time. Everyone, we all made mistakes… We've just got to try and move on. I know it's hard for everyone,” he said.

Recent revelations by several players, including a 4,000-word piece by Cameron Bancroft in The West Australian, threw fresh light on the scandal, with Bancroft specifically alleging that Lehmann and then bowling coach David Saker had agreed to the plot during the tea break on the second day of the second Test.

“I can't remember that conversation. Again, eight and a half years ago. You'd have to ask those people… That's the issue. I have my version and that's where I stand,” said Lehmann when asked about Bancroft's account.

Lehmann, who resigned in the aftermath of the scandal, also spoke about the mental and emotional toll of the incident. “Eight and a half years ago, and I don't like talking about this sort of scenario, but I went to a really dark place. As dark a place as you can think about.

“It took me, and this is just me, probably three or four years to actually get back to some sort of normality. To the stage where we are now, I'm not going back to that. I'm trying to move forward. I'm not going back,” he said.
Describing the period as “traumatic”, Lehmann called for an end to the debate and urged people to respect the fact that “everyone's going through a tough time”.

“I feel for everyone at the moment and their families. Social media has been so vitriolic. The hatred is there. It's just unbelievable. I've never seen anything like it since 2018. And the trauma for everyone is there to see again. I know people aren't in a great place.
“Some of the things that are being said are just outright hurtful to a lot of people… Yes, there were mistakes. You apologise as best you can, you try and move on.

“I can only speak for me. I wish we did things differently and we didn't push the boundaries too far. We didn't get to the stage where we got to. I've just got to take responsibility for that. That's where I'm at,” he added.

news.title: Allround Nikhil Chaudhary puts Australia 1-0 up
news.excerpt: Jack Edwards came up with a vital cameo towards the end to seal Australia's win at the MCG
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Nikhil Chaudhary starred with an all-round show as Australia edged out England by three wickets in a thrilling last-over finish at the MCG to go 1-0 up in the five-match T20I series. Chaudhary picked 2-21 with the ball before making his T20I career-best 66 off 38 balls to set up a successful penultimate-ball finish.

After Australian captain Mitchell Marsh won the toss and elected to bowl, England suffered an immediate setback when opener Phil Salt was dismissed for a duck off the very first ball of the match. Aneurin Donald fell for 10 at the start of the third over, leaving England reeling at 13 for 2.

Captain Harry Brook then launched a fierce counterattack, capitalizing on two early dropped chances to smash 65 off just 28 balls, including four boundaries and half a dozen sixes. That included a hat-trick of maximums off Riley Meredith in the fourth over. Brook reached his half-century in 20 deliveries and added 97 runs for the third wicket with Tom Banton, propelling England to 74 for 2 inside the six-over powerplay and past 100 in the eighth over.

Australia regained momentum through Chaudhary, who dismissed Brook - caught by Sam Harper at 110 for 3. Ben Dwarshuis removed Banton for 39 off 22 balls in the next over, and Chaudhary then trapped Sam Curran to finish with impressive figures of 2 for 21. Despite Australia dropping six catches in the field, disciplined middle-over bowling restricted England's scoring rate. Jordan Cox (27 off 20) and Liam Dawson (17 off 14) stitched together a crucial 30-run seventh-wicket stand. Dawson was run out off the final ball as England finished with 187 for 9.

Australia got off to a sedate start in the chase, with Liam Dawson squeezing out two tight overs and an early wicket of Jake Fraser-McGurk in the opening over. Sam Harper injected early momentum with a brisk 32 off 15 balls, striking four fours and two sixes during a 50-run partnership with Marsh. After Harper fell to Henry Crocombe at the end of the Powerplay, at 53/2, Chaudhary anchored the chase alongside Marsh.

The Australian captain chipped in a vital 37 off 32 balls before falling to Sam Curran in the 11th over. Chaudhary, meanwhile, continued his all-round heroics, bringing up a 32-ball fifty and keeping Australia in contention alongside Tim David.

A late collapse of 4 for 25 then threatened to derail the hosts: Adil Rashid removed David, Will Jacks claimed two wickets in the 17th over to dismiss Lachlan Shaw and Joel Davies, and Jamie Overton had Chaudhary caught by Donald for 66 off 38 balls at the end of the 18th over, leaving Australia at 168 for 7.

Needing 11 runs off the final over bowled by Curran, Jack Edwards sealed the victory in dramatic fashion - hitting the first ball over fine leg for six, running two braces, and steering a full toss through point for four on the penultimate ball.

Brief scores: England 187/9 in 20 overs (Harry Brook 65, Tom Banton 39, Jordan Cox 27; Nikhil Chaudhary 2-21, Jack Edwards 2-27) lost to Australia 191/7 in 19.5 overs (Nikhil Chaudhary 66, Mitchell Marsh 37, Sam Harper 32, Jack Edwards 25*; Will Jacks 2-29) by 3 wickets

news.title: Mushfiqur Rahim ruled out of second South Africa Test
news.excerpt: Mushfiqur will miss the second Test in centurion due to a groin injury
news.author: Atif Azam
body: Bangladesh have suffered a huge blow ahead of the second Test against South Africa as veteran batter Mushfiqur Rahim has been ruled out after sustaining a groin injury.
The second Test against South Africa starts at Centurion on November 23.
While his team members were busy preparing for the second Test at Centurion on Saturday, Mushfiqur was found sitting on the bench.

"Mushfiqur complained of acute pain in the left groin region during the first Test match. Following the Test, he underwent an MRI scan and the results confirmed some inflammation and irritation around the bony pelvis,” national team physio Bayjedul Islam Khan said.
“He requires immediate rest and targeted rehabilitation to manage the stress response and prevent further aggravation and is unavailable for the second Test,” he added.
Bangladesh lost the first Test at the Wanderers by nine wickets and will be looking to level the series when they take on the hosts in Centurion.

news.title: Smith, Lee, Trenaman help Hurricanes break duck
news.excerpt: Meanwhile, Sydney Sixers sealed their playoff berth with a win over Perth Scorchers
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Sydney Thunder vs Hobart Hurricanes

Eight games in, the Hobart Hurricanes finally got on the board, registering their first win of the season by beating the Sydney Thunder in Hobart. A three-wicket haul from Linsey Smith followed by an unbeaten 55 from Rachel Trenaman saw the Hurricanes register a comfortable eight-wicket win.

Opting to bowl first, the Hurricanes managed to keep Georgia Voll quiet and had her dismissed off the last ball of the Powerplay. Phoebe Litchfield provided early impetus but was out offering a return catch to Linsey Smith in the sixth over.

Anika Learoyd and Heather Knight got off to starts but were both dismissed for 18 by Lauren Smith and Linsey Smith respectively. It was a 56-run stand between Nadine de Klerk (36*) and Tahlia Wilson (29) that really moved the needle for the Thunder. Linsey Smith returned to break the partnership in the 19th over by dismissing Wilson as the Thunder finished with 150 for 5.

In reply, the Hurricanes’ openers got the team off to a brisk start, making 40 for 0 by the end of the Powerplay. Lizelle Lee struck three fours and four sixes in her 22-ball 42 before falling to Samantha Bates in the sixth over. Kate Pelle then fell to Jemma Barsby for a run-a-ball 18 in the eighth.

An unbeaten 80-run partnership followed as Trenaman and Nicola Carey batted with freedom. Eight boundaries were struck in the space of 13 deliveries starting with the first ball of the 14th over as the Hurricanes got over the line with nearly five overs to spare.
The loss throws a spanner in the works for the Thunder who are now placed fifth on the points table with three wins from eight games.

Brief Scores: Sydney Thunder 150/5 in 20 overs (Nadine de Klerk 36*, Tahlia Wilson 29; Linsey Smith 3-19) lost to Hobart Hurricanes 151/2 in 15.1 overs (Rachel Trenaman 55*, Lizelle Lee 42; Jemma Barsby 1-24) by 8 wickets.
Sydney Sixers vs Perth Scorchers

Sydney Sixers registered their seventh win of the season and became the first team to qualify for the playoffs after beating the Perth Scorchers by four wickets (DLS) in Sydney on Saturday (November 21). A three-wicket haul from captain Ash Gardner helped restrict the Scorchers to 142 before a fifty from Sophia Dunkley saw the Sixers chase a revised target of 120 after the game was affected by rain.

Asked to bat first, the Scorchers started slow and were reduced to 68 for 5 by the 11th. Caoimhe Bray bowled Katie Mack before Amelia Kerr dismissed Sophie Devine and Mikayla Hinkley off successive deliveries.

There was a brief recovery through Beth Mooney and Chloe Piparo but Gardner dismissed both set batters in quick succession. She first had a well-set Mooney out stumped for 21 in the eighth over before holding on to a return catch offered by Piparo in her next over. Freya Kemp made a fighting 30-ball 43 but became Gardner’s third victim in the 18th over. The Scorchers eventually finished with 142 for 7 in 20 overs.

In pursuit, Dunkley made a blazing start, striking three sixes and four fours before play was stopped due to rain at the end of the fourth over. The chase was reduced to 16 overs, with the Sixers now chasing a revised target of 120. By then, the Sixers had already lost Ellyse Perry, and Ruby Strange struck right after the break, trapping Kerr LBW.

Dunkley and Gardner shared a brief 23-run stand before the Scorchers barged back into the contest by taking four wickets in the space of four overs while conceding just 20 runs. With the Sixers at 86 for 6, Sarah Coyte and Courtney Sippel added an unbroken 34 to finish the job in the 15th over. The loss was only the Scorchers’ second of the season and they remain well placed at second place on the points table with two games to go.

Brief Scores: Perth Scorchers 142/7 in 20 overs (Freya Kemp 43, Chloe Piparo 27; Ash Gardner 3-24) lost to Sydney Sixers 120/6 in 14.5 overs (Sophia Dunkley 54, Sarah Coyte 18*; Sophie Devine 2-22) by 4 wickets (DLS).

news.title: ‘Not the colour we’d have liked’: Jacob Oram rues Wellington pitch
news.excerpt: New Zealand's bowling coach conceded that the hosts had perhaps read too much into the grass on Day 1 having gone in without a frontline spinner
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: New Zealand bowling coach Jacob Oram had hoped for a Basin Reserve pitch with more life in it. The grass, 15 millimeters of it at the start of play on Day 1, has quickly browned, while the pace and bounce the venue is known for never quite arrived. After India reached 486/4 with a lead of 118 on Day 3 of the first Test, Oram conceded that New Zealand had perhaps read too much into the grass and gone in without a full-time spinner.

"That's a great question, and I think you know the answer to that,” Oram said on not picking a frontline spinner. “Look, grass isn't the issue. There's plenty of grass out there, but it's just probably not the colour we would have liked. And yeah, we fell into it [the trap] as well. It's a very nice wicket to bat on.

“Thank God for [Henry] Nicholls and [Glenn] Phillips for getting us a nice total, but once guys get in, the pace and bounce that we've become accustomed to here is not quite there. It feels like a day or two too early in terms of the lack of pace and bounce. But that's not the reason we're behind either. The wicket is not what we expected, but it's not the complete answer to why we're 100 runs behind.”
The former New Zealand all-rounder was careful not to blame the groundstaff, but said it was the lack of bounce, more than the lack of movement, that had made life hard for his bowlers.

"I don't want to throw too many stones, because I wouldn't want to be a groundsman, and you're dealing with natural variables down below and up top,” Oram said. “But I think guys can handle minimal sideways movement if there's some good bounce and carry as well. When you're suddenly not getting much laterally, and you're bending your back and running in and it's just dying in the surface, that's when it becomes, 'What am I working with here?' Basically, then it comes down to attrition and accuracy, which I thought we did really, really well. I know they still scored at four an over, which makes it look like a really bad day. But I thought we did an admirable job, for sure."
No New Zealand bowler had a harder day than Jacob Duffy. He went for 181 runs in 29 overs, and his only wicket came in the last over of the day, when he bowled Shubman Gill two short of a hundred.

"Jacob Duffy's fine,” Oram said. “We try not to get too high when things are good and we try not to get too low when things haven't gone our way. Today, if you just look at the scoreboard, it's not his day, but he's had way too many good days in the last two seasons for one day to suddenly put him in the depths of despair. So he'll be okay.

“At the same time, he knows he's got areas to work on and improve, but he's not the only one in the dressing room. Even last season, when he won the Sir Richard Hadlee Medal, he was working on things. I know right now you can say it's lip service because he's had a bad day, but the guy is always working hard. That's how these guys stay where they are."
KL Rahul, who made 136, said they would be counting on tired legs rather than help from the surface when they bowl again. India need a win to stay in contention for the World Test Championship final.

"When we saw the wicket when we first got here, we didn't think it would play like this," Rahul admitted. "We expected it to be very different. You expect the ball to do a lot more, but it's a pretty good wicket if you apply yourself and play out good spells. I think we spent a lot of time playing on that wicket. It'll take a lot of hard work for the wickets in the second innings. But we're counting on the fact that if we keep them on the park for long enough, with some tired legs, that's when you make mistakes. That's the beauty of Test cricket. I'm not saying the wicket's completely flat and there's nothing happening.

"There's always an odd ball that keeps low, the odd ball that is seaming. Even when I was batting on 130, they were beating my bat sometimes. If it was India, I would have been confident that the wear and tear on days four and five is a lot more. I'm not sure how this wicket historically plays. It would be great if we can get them all out in 50-60 overs, but realistically, maybe give ourselves a good three, three and a half sessions to bowl at them and have a crack."
With two days left, Oram did not expect much help from the surface, whatever the weather.

"I think this is a ground of two ends,” Oram said. “I don't want to say it's complete attack and defend, but obviously it's a lot easier when the wind is behind you. But for me, it's more about what's happening on the surface, and at the moment, it doesn't seem to be breaking up. There is grass out there. It's just not green grass. I would be surprised if it breaks up. The footmarks might play a part, and the odd one has felt like it's kept low for sure. But at the moment, it still feels like a good wicket to bat on."

news.title: Rahul credits ‘six-seven months of homework' for maiden ton in NZ
news.excerpt: Rahul also admitted that reverting to the opening role after some time in the middle-order helped his rhythm
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: KL Rahul's first Test innings in New Zealand had been months in the making. The opener made 136 on Day 3 of the Wellington Test, becoming only the second Asian opener after Saeed Anwar to score Test hundreds in all four SENA countries, and said afterwards how he had been "thinking about Test cricket in New Zealand for the last six or seven months."

"Obviously, when you play Test cricket for that long, when you finish your career, you want to at least get that opportunity to challenge yourself in different countries and play against the best attacks,” Rahul said. “New Zealand has been a country where a lot of batters have struggled to get runs, and it is difficult conditions. So I wanted to play a Test match here. I wanted to play a lot more, but unfortunately I haven't played here before this. So when I got the opportunity, I wanted to make the most of it. That's why I decided to come in early as well, just to get used to the conditions, because I have no prior experience of coming to New Zealand and playing red-ball cricket.

“I've been thinking about Test cricket in New Zealand for the last six or seven months, trying to do my homework, trying to see the guys that have scored runs here and how they've been able to achieve that. So a lot of prep, a lot of homework. And once you've ticked all those boxes, it becomes slightly easier when you play the game.”
Part of that homework was watching footage of batters who had succeeded at the venues here.

"I watched the last few years of Test cricket here,” Rahul elaborated. “England played here, Australia played here, West Indies were here recently. So I asked the analysts to send me some videos of guys who've got runs here. Joe Root was there, Harry Brook scored a lot of runs, especially top-order batters. I don't think I can do what Harry Brook does, but it was interesting to see that there are different ways of getting runs and different types of players have been able to succeed here.

“It just gave me a little confidence that it's not impossible to get runs in New Zealand. It requires a very clear game plan. So I went back to speaking to my coach and figuring out what could be the best game plan for me, and we worked on that for a good four or five months."
Rahul also spoke about how going back to being a Test opener helped him settle into a rhythm, and how watching other opening batters helped him find his mojo back.

“It helped a lot,” Rahul said. “There were 15-18 months when I didn’t open, played in the middle order, and then I had gotten into a habit of feeling bat on ball. When I went back to opening, I consciously tried to work on it in the nets. Sometimes less balls on the bat approach during sessions.

“Over the years, I've watched other openers and how they've been successful. Somebody like Alastair Cook. I used to watch him from slips and see how he batted. He left a lot of deliveries and made the bowlers bowl at him. It's the basics of cricket but sometimes that’s the most difficult bit. As I've gotten slightly older, I've worked on that again, and it's helped me a lot with opening."

Rahul had an early escape on Day 2, when New Zealand chose not to review an lbw appeal from Matt Henry that ball-tracking showed would have hit the stumps. Asked whether he owed Tom Latham a hug, he pointed to someone else.

"No, that's probably Glenn Phillips; buy him a few drinks after the game,” Rahul said with a smile. “And also Tom Latham, because he had the decision to make. When it happened, I honestly thought it might have hit me outside the line of off stump. That was my feeling. But some of the fielders felt it hit my bat. Those 15 seconds were probably the slowest 15 seconds of my life. I kept hoping that people would listen to Glenn Phillips, because he kept saying I smashed it. So thanks, GP, for that."

Asked what had changed in the last two years to lift his Test average, Rahul's first answer was brief. "Runs. I scored more runs," he said, before elaborating further. "Honestly, I don't think much has changed. I've always prepared the same way ever since I got my Test cap. I've worked as hard as I am working currently. It's just that the runs weren't coming, and yes, there were some technical issues as well, and maybe I could have had a better game plan. I don't think technique was the issue, but how I thought about the game, all of that has evolved over time. The more you play, you recognise the mistakes you make and how you can get better. With experience, I've been lucky that I can turn that around. But there's a lot more left for me to do."

news.title: Rizwan, Saim, Shan Masood left out as PCB hands format-wise contracts to 38
news.excerpt: Babar Azam and Salman Ali Agha get Test and ODI deals, while 19 youngsters are handed development contracts
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: The Pakistan Cricket Board has announced a new central contracts structure for the senior men's team, switching to a format-based system for the cycle running until June 30, 2027. 38 players are covered under the new structure, with 19 falling under the Development category. The new system replaces last year's category-based list, which ran from Category B to D.

Test captain Babar Azam and former T20I skipper Salman Agha are the only players to be awarded a Test and ODI contract, while Mohammad Abbas, Azan Awais, Sajid Khan and Saud Shakeel have been handed a Test contract alone. No player has been offered a contract across all three formats.

A host of players, including recent Test debutants Razaullah, Tayyab Arif, Mohammad Taha, Ghazi Ghori and Saqib Khan, have received Development contracts. ODI skipper Shaheen Shah Afridi has been handed an ODI and T20I contract, while T20I captain Sahibzada Farhan has been awarded a T20I contract alone.

Wicketkeeper Mohammad Rizwan, who has found himself embroiled in off-field controversies and was sent home midway through the tour of England, is the most noteworthy omission from the list. Rizwan held a Category B contract last year.

Rizwan is one of 13 players from last year's list who do not feature this time. Saim Ayub and Hasan Ali, both in Category B last year, also miss out, as does Shan Masood. Abdullah Shafique, Mohammad Haris, Mohammad Nawaz, Noman Ali, Hussain Talat, Khurram Shahzad, Khushdil Shah, Mohammad Abbas Afridi and Mohammad Wasim Jnr are the others left out.
PCB Men’s Central Contracts (Until 30 June, 2027)
Test and ODI: Babar Azam, Salman Agha
Test: Azan Awais, Mohammad Abbas, Sajid Khan, Saud Shakeel
ODI and T20I: Abrar Ahmed, Arafat Minhas, Fakhar Zaman, Faheem Ashraf, Haris Rauf, Shaheen Shah Afridi
T20I: Hasan Nawaz, Maaz Sadaqat, Salman Mirza, Naseem Shah, Sahibzada Farhan, Shadab Khan, Usman Tariq

Development: Abdul Samad, Abdullah Fazal, Ahmed Daniyal, Ali Raza, Farhan Yousaf, Hunain Shah, Mohammad Taha, Tayyab Arif, Ghazi Ghori, Mohammad Imran Randhawa, Razaullah, Saad Baig, Saad Masood, Sameer Minhas, Saqib Khan, Shahzaib Khan, Shamyl Hussain, Sufyan Moqim, Ubaid Shah

news.title: Rahul ton, Gill 98 headline productive batting day for India
news.excerpt: The visitors scored 327 runs for the loss of three wickets on the third day in Wellington
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: KL Rahul struck a hundred in his maiden Test outing in New Zealand, while Shubman Gill agonisingly missed out on one during a productive day for India in Wellington. It was the first time that each of India's top five scored fifty-plus in an overseas Test innings, with Rahul's 136 and Gill's 98 leading the way, alongside Devdutt Padikkal's 80. India ended the third day's play at 486 for 4, leading by 118, with Rishabh Pant unbeaten on 55.

Matt Henry and Nathan Smith began the proceedings on Day 3, with New Zealand having come out with a clear plan - bowl tight lines with the 'keeper up to the stumps on a pitch expected to get slower and lower. It was a battle of patience with five of the first six overs being maidens, but the Indians also capitalised when they sensed boundary opportunities. Kyle Jamieson and Jacob Duffy came on next, with the 'keeper staying back this time, but they weren't able to make inroads as the second wicket pair built a solid partnership and got through the first hour unscathed.

The strike rotation also got better as the session progressed, with Rahul and Padikkal helping India past the 200 mark in the second hour before the left-hander went past 50 for the third time in his last four innings. For the first time in the innings, Tom Latham introduced spin in the form of Glenn Phillips, but the offspinner went for runs - including the first six of the match when Rahul cleared long-on to extend the partnership past 100. Rahul moved into the 90s with a four past covers off Phillips. Rahul and Padikkal ensured a wicketless session, with India scoring 80 runs in 27 overs.

The toil continued for the New Zealand bowlers post Lunch, with nothing happening off the wicket, as Rahul and Padikkal added to their partnership. Early in the second session, Rahul brought up his 13th Test hundred with a single off Duffy, soon after which Henry Nicholls put down a chance at gully to give Padikkal a reprieve. The left-hander capitalised as he struck regular boundaries and the second wicket pair extended their partnership past 150. Phillips and Rachin Ravindra bowled in tandem for a few overs but no damage was done as wickets continued to evade New Zealand in the hour after Lunch.

The second new ball was taken as soon as it was due and New Zealand finally got a breakthrough. Padikkal, who was looking good for his third three-figure score in as many Tests, fell 20 short of it, bowled by a terrific delivery from Jamieson. Meanwhile, the Indian batters had to deal with low bounce every now and then, as Rahul and Gill took their side past 300. Gill got his first four via an edge off Duffy before striking three more fours in an over off the same bowler. The partnership moved to 49 as India finished the second session with 105 runs in 27 overs, bringing the deficit down to 24.

Post Tea, New Zealand bowlers began with tight lines but the boundaries started coming soon enough, including a six for Gill that took him past 50 and India into the lead. This marked only the second instance of all India's top four getting fifty-plus scores in a Test innings outside Asia - the first one coming against West Indies in Basseterre in 2006. Rahul and Gill added 91 in quick time before the former dragged on a Smith delivery playing away from his body. New Zealand lost a review when they thought Pant was caught behind in his attempt to hook Duffy, only for the replays to show it came off the shoulder. India then used the DRS successfully as Gill got an lbw decision reversed in Smith's over, with the visitors crossing 400 soon after.

Every time New Zealand looked to build some pressure, Gill found a way to release it, scoring a four and a six off Phillips in different overs as he moved into the 80s. A half-century stand was raised, with Pant contributing only 15 in that as he continued to hand the strike back to his skipper. The wicketkeeper-batter took until the 39th delivery he faced for his first four, which came off a top-edged pull. The boundaries started flowing off his bat soon after, with the big hits also coming as he struck two sixes and a four in a Duffy over to take the lead past 100. Pant got to his half-century, off 55 balls, with another four off Duffy. The century stand followed, with Pant having contributed 55.

142 runs came in the final session, in 32 overs, as India got 327 runs in the day's play. And it was a forgettable day for Duffy, who had conceded 179 runs in 28 overs. But he made amends by taking Gill's wicket in the final over of the day, going through the gate to hit the stumps as the disappointed Indian captain walked back two short of a hundred. New Zealand, however, lost their last review going up for a leg-before shout against Anshul Kamboj on what was the final ball of the day.
Brief scores: New Zealand 368 trail India 486/4 (KL Rahul 136, Shubman Gill 98, Yashasvi Jaiswal 85, Devdutt Padikkal 80, Rishabh Pant 55*) by 118 runs.

news.title: CA board unanimously backs Cummins as Test captain
news.excerpt: CA chair David Boon and chief executive Todd Greenberg met Cummins, discussing several issues including "his welfare, support required for the team and the forthcoming series against New Zealand"
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Cricket Australia's board has given its unanimous backing to Pat Cummins as Test captain, after a meeting called to address the renewed speculation over the 2018 tour of South Africa.

CA chair David Boon and chief executive Todd Greenberg met Cummins in Sydney on Friday. They discussed several issues including “his welfare, support required for the team and the forthcoming series against New Zealand” according to a board media release. The statement came after Josh Hazlewood said he would have to think about his own future in the side if Cummins was fired as Test captain.

"We are absolutely determined to steward Australian Cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn," Boon said. "That's what the independent Forum we announced this week is about and the Board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there. We will be publishing the Terms of Reference in due course.

"We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa. We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised."
Cummins said he would attend the forum, which CA set up this week for players and staff from the 2018 tour to give their accounts in private.

"It meant a lot to speak with David and Todd on Friday. Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly," Cummins said. "David and Todd have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.

"I support the Forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what's needed. Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."
The first of four Tests against New Zealand starts in Perth on December 9.

news.title: Hazlewood denies sandpaper knowledge, hints at walking away if Cummins is removed
news.excerpt: Josh Hazlewood stood by the bowlers' position that they were never part of the plan, and left the door open to stepping away from the Test side should Pat Cummins lose the captaincy
news.author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: "Two things stand out for me from what's been said. Was I an architect in the plan to tamper with the ball with sandpaper? And was I aware sandpaper or foreign substances being used on the field? The answer is no."

Josh Hazlewood, in an interview to News Corp, has given his account of the 2018 ball-tampering saga for the first time since it’s resurfaced in recent weeks. He stood by the bowlers' position that they were never part of the plan, and left the door open to stepping away from the Test side should Pat Cummins lose the captaincy.
"I think I'd have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you'd have to think about it, yeah," he said when asked whether he would consider quitting.

Usman Khawaja set this off with his autobiography, Sabr, in which he wrote that every member of the side knew sandpaper was being used. Cummins dismissed that as "complete and utter nonsense" over a 68-minute press conference. Bancroft then sided with Khawaja in a 4,000-word statement that put the bowlers' long-standing denials back in the spotlight.
Hazlewood said he trusts the account he gave investigators in the days after Cape Town more than anything said since.

"We were interviewed straight after [Cape Town] and I trust what I said in that two-three hour interrogation more than anything because it was in the day or two after," he said. "It was fresh in my mind at that point. When it boils down to it I think those two points are crucial. Assuming everyone knows and actually knowing everyone knows, that gap is huge. That's a big chasm."
Hazlewood threw his weight behind his captain, who’s been under pressure after Bancroft’s statement.

"It feels like it's been a bit of a pile on the last few days from different people," Hazlewood said. "I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain. To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that is never going to happen again, I think is just a remarkable job. He's a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you'd hear the same response. I think if we turned up for the first Test and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."

In his statement, Bancroft said he worked on the ball with sandpaper over after over in Port Elizabeth while checking with the bowlers about reverse swing. Hazlewood accepted that the questions were asked. He did not accept what they are now taken to mean.

"It's definitely a normal interaction and I read that part [in Bancroft's statement]. I have no doubt that he was asking us those things about the ball reversing. There's not one point in his statement where he says 'Oh, I'm doing this with sandpaper.'"

Nor did he read anything into the meeting on the third morning at which, by Bancroft's account, he was praised for his work on the ball. "Looking after the ball is crucial in Test cricket especially in conditions like that, but he hasn't mentioned sandpaper, he hasn't mentioned taking something on the field," Hazlewood said. "It's just well done on looking after the ball."
On the ball itself, he added: "I never remember looking at the ball and going, 'wow, this is not natural deterioration'. And obviously the umpires didn't either."

Khawaja and Bancroft both say the plan was first raised in the dressing room at Tea on Day 2 in Port Elizabeth. Hazlewood questioned how far that conversation could have carried. The room was "quite long and thin", he said, and with only 20 minutes before going back out, the bowlers would mostly have been at their end getting ready. In his view it was a "genuine assumption" that the two groups kept apart.

The Cape Town room had a dividing wall of its own, which he said cut the space "70-30", and he was on the other side from Bancroft and Khawaja. On Bancroft's claim that David Saker, then the bowling coach, told him to carry on with the ball, Hazlewood said: "I honestly can't comment on whether that conversation happened or not. I had no knowledge of it."

Bancroft, Khawaja and Chadd Sayers also recall the players agreeing to take collective responsibility in a meeting after play in Cape Town. Hazlewood said he does not remember it. He also called the bans handed to Bancroft, David Warner and Steve Smith "ridiculous".

Cricket Australia has said it will not reopen its investigation, instead setting up an independent committee to re-hear testimonies from players and support staff who were part of Australia’s squad during the 2018 tour of South Africa, which it hopes will serve as a ‘circuit-breaker’ to the ball-tampering saga.
